title: News site
like: a news site like the BBC or CNN
brief: You run a news site. Millions read the same few stories, and when something big happens almost everyone opens the same page in the same minute. Editors publish all day, and readers expect fresh headlines.

clarify.q: How fresh must the front page be?
clarify.a: A minute behind is fine. A headline that is an hour old is not.
Mostly not. Only a small group of subscribers and editors sign in.

clarify.q: Are most readers reading different stories?
clarify.a: No. A handful of stories get most of the views, especially during breaking news.

clarify.q: What happens if the site goes down during a big story?
clarify.a: Readers go elsewhere, and the editors are very unhappy. Breaking news is exactly when it must work.

notes: A page is about 4 KB of data per request in the game (approx.); images are served separately.

numbers.label: Page views per second at peak
Page views per second in a breaking-news spike
Different stories getting most of the views

hints: Almost everyone reads the same few pages. How could you answer them without asking a database each time?
A CDN with a short cache time (a minute or so) serves hot pages to everyone and still keeps headlines fresh. Collapsing misses protects you when the cache is empty.
Try: readers -> CDN -> a small group of app servers -> database. Search goes to a search index.

editorial.summary: A news site is a read-heavy site with a tiny number of very hot pages. Let the CDN absorb the crowd with a one-minute cache, and keep the database for editors and for cache misses. The classic failure is a cold cache and a huge crowd arriving together.

designs.name: Short-lived CDN cache
designs.why: The CDN holds every page for about a minute and merges simultaneous misses, so the app servers see a trickle even in a spike. A search index handles search without hurting the database.

tradeoffs: A one-minute cache means a correction can take up to a minute to appear. Clearing the cache on publish fixes that for important stories, at the cost of extra work for editors.
Collapsing misses stops the stampede after a cold start, but one slow origin request now makes every reader of that page wait.
Autoscaling helps with a slow ramp, but a 25 times spike arrives in seconds. The CDN, not the servers, is what saves you.
A replica is a little behind the main database. For a news page that is fine. For an editor who just hit publish it is not.
editorial.realWorld: Big news sites often serve 95 to 99 percent of page views from CDN and edge caches (approx.), so the origin sees nearly the same load on a normal day and on a record-breaking one.

correctness.prompt: News site: The same request is delivered twice, and a worker can crash after saving it. What uniqueness constraint and transaction would keep one durable result?
correctness.discussion: Choose a stable business operation id and enforce a unique constraint in the authoritative store. Insert the id, apply the change and save its result in one transaction. A retry returns that result. Recording the id before the change can lose work after a crash; recording it afterwards can apply the change twice. If work continues through a queue, commit an outbox entry in the same transaction and deduplicate at each consumer.

fields.label: The server commits a change, then crashes before replying. The client retries. What happens?
options: Commit the operation id, effect and result atomically; return that result on retry
Record the id first, then apply the change in a separate write
fields.explanation: Recording the id separately can either lose an operation or apply it twice. The effect and deduplication result must commit together.

fields.label: The server acknowledges a write just before its storage fails. Which evidence meets the stated recovery point?
options: A queued backup request with no completed durable copy
A measured replication or backup gap of at most 60 seconds, with a tested replay plan
fields.explanation: A scheduled copy is not a completed copy. Match acknowledgement and recovery to the stated loss boundary.
